ppt-images-037.pdfWording:
Raw images will come in wildly different dimensions/aspect ratios, especially if sourced from multiple places (web scraping + manual capture + public datasets).
Methods:
Simple resize/stretch - fast, but distorts aspect ratio if the original isn't square.
Resize + crop - preserves aspect ratio by cutting off edges.
Resize + pad ("letterboxing") - preserves aspect ratio by adding blank/black borders instead of cropping content out.

ppt-images-038.pdfWording: Rescaling pixel values (raw 0–255 integers) into a smaller, standardized numeric range — commonly 0–1 (divide by 255) or standardized to mean 0, std 1 (subtract dataset mean, divide by dataset standard deviation, often per color channel).
ppt-images-038.clarification: The slide groups min-max scaling and standardization under Normalization. Standardization uses a mean and standard deviation; it does not force a Gaussian distribution.

ppt-images-039.pdfWording:
RGB → Grayscale: reduces 3 color channels to 1, cutting file size/computation — used when color isn't a meaningful signal for the task (e.g., document text recognition, X-ray analysis where color is nonexistent/irrelevant anyway).
RGB → HSV: separates color (hue) from intensity/brightness (saturation/value) — sometimes used when you want the model to be more robust to lighting changes, since brightness and color become independent dimensions instead of tangled together.

ppt-images-042.pdfWording:
In a class-imbalanced dataset, one label is considerably more common than the other.
Solution:
[STEP 1] Downsample the majority class: you shrink the majority class down to be closer in size to the minority class.
[STEP 2] Upweighting: Instead of duplicating the X CLASS images back, you tell the model: "every time you see an X CLASS example, treat it as if it were worth Y Value examples, not 1"
ppt-images-042.clarification: These are the slide’s proposed techniques, not a mandatory sequence for every imbalanced dataset.

ppt-images-064.pdfWording:
1.Load a pretrained model. Choose a CNN trained on a large dataset (ResNet, MobileNet, or EfficientNet). Remove its original classification layer.
2.Add a new classification layer matching your number of classes.
3.Freeze the pretrained layers. Their weights stay fixed. This preserves the general visual features (edges, textures, shapes) and reduces computation.
4.Train the new classification head on your dataset. It learns to map the frozen features to your new labels.
5.Fine-tune (optional). After the new head has converged, unfreeze some or all pretrained layers and continue training with a very low learning rate.

ppt-images-072.pdfWording:
- overall correctness
- measures the proportion of all predictions that the model classified correctly, including both positive and negative predictions.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
“Out of ALL the predictions, how many did the model get right?”

ppt-images-073.pdfWording:
- trustworthiness of positive predictions
- measures the proportion of positive predictions that are actually positive.
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
“When the model says YES, how often is it actually right?”

ppt-images-074.pdfWording:
- coverage of actual positives
- measures the proportion of actual positive cases that the model correctly identifies.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
“Out of all the things that were actually YES, how many did the model find?”

ppt-images-075.pdfWording:
- balancing Precision and Recall
- the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall.
- provides a single measure that balances the model's ability to make reliable positive predictions and identify actual positive cases.
F1-Score = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)
OR F1-Score = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN)

The process of identifying and keeping only the most relevant input variables to improve model performance. Irrelevant or redundant features introduce noise, increase computational overhead, and risk overfitting—a problem known as the curse of dimensionality—which reduces a model's ability to generalize to new data.
By removing useless variables using statistical tests, correlation analysis, or algorithm feature importance, you streamline training time, reduce complexity, and boost prediction accuracy.
ppt-datasets-056.clarification: Overfitting and the curse of dimensionality are related concerns, but they are not the same phenomenon.

ppt-datasets-093.pdfWording:
MAE (Mean Absolute Error): Average absolute difference between predicted and actual values.
MSE (Mean Squared Error): Average squared difference: MSE = (1/n) Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ).
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error): Square root of MSE, in the same units as the target.
R (Coefficient of Determination): Proportion of variance in the target explained by the model; ranges from 0 to 1 (higher is better).
ppt-datasets-093.clarification: The PDF omits the square in MSE: the correct formula is MSE = (1/n) Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². RMSE = sqrt(MSE). Coefficient of determination is R², and it can be negative; it is not always limited to 0–1.
